title: The beginning (Mark 1:1–8)
hook: no birth story: Mark starts with a voice in the wilderness and a man in camel hair
carry: the beginning of the good news

segments.voice: Yesterday: a rule of life, and the close of camp three. Your line was small rules keep big loves. Are your three lines where you can see them? Now camp four: the text, read in order. Day one hundred fifty-seven.
screen: `SMALL RULES KEEP BIG LOVES.` → `CAMP FOUR: THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: If you know the Christmas story, you might expect a book about Jesus to start there: the manger, the shepherds, the star. Mark doesn't. Mark has no manger. No angels singing. No wise men. No baby at all. Mark, the shortest of the four gospels and, most scholars think, the earliest, skips all of it. It opens with one line, like a title, and then drops you straight into the desert, where a wild-looking man in camel hair, eating locusts and wild honey, is shouting at crowds by a river. For the next several weeks, we're going to read Mark from the beginning, in order, a few verses at a time. Today, the very first word Mark uses for his book.
screen: `NO MANGER, NO ANGELS, NO BABY.` → `ONE LINE, LIKE A TITLE.` → `A MAN IN CAMEL HAIR.`

segments.voice: Gospel. Here's how Mark begins, in the King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." Gospel is an Old English word, godspel, good news. It translates the Greek euangelion. And here's what first readers would have heard. In the Roman world, euangelion was the word for big public announcements: a victory in battle, a new emperor. An inscription from a city in what's now Turkey even calls the emperor Augustus's birthday the beginning of good news for the world. So when Mark calls his book the beginning of the good news of Jesus, it's a bold claim. The real good news, he's saying, is this. Then Mark quotes the prophets. "The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." And there's the voice: John the Baptist. Mark gives us his outfit and his menu: "John was clothed with camel's hair, and with a girdle of a skin about his loins; and he did eat locusts and wild honey." That's not a random detail. The prophet Elijah was remembered as a hairy man with a leather belt, and many expected Elijah to come back before God's great day. Mark's readers would have noticed. Crowds come from all over Judea and Jerusalem to be baptized by John in the Jordan. But John points away from himself: "There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose." Eight verses, and Mark is already racing. That's his style. He doesn't linger. He wants you to feel that something is starting, right now. The beginning of the good news.
screen: `GODSPEL, EUANGELION — GOOD NEWS.` · `A WORD FOR EMPERORS' NEWS.` · `A VOICE IN THE WILDERNESS.` · `CAMEL HAIR, LIKE ELIJAH.` · then, large: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the first eight verses of Mark aloud. If you have a Bible or an app nearby, open to Mark chapter one. If not, just hold the first line in your mind. Read slowly, out loud, even in a whisper. Notice how fast it moves: a title, a prophecy, a voice, a man in camel hair, crowds, a river, and then someone mightier coming. When you finish, sit with whichever image stayed with you. If you pray, you can offer it back. If you don't, just let it sit. The bell holds the time.
Gospel. From Old English for good news, translating the Greek euangelion, a word once used for an emperor's announcements.
Your line: the beginning of the good news. Today, read Mark chapter one, verses one to eight, out loud. Day one hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: In many churches, a passage from the Gospels is read aloud at every service, often with the congregation standing, and many Christians read through a gospel like Mark in order, a few verses a day.

fork.setup: you're John the Baptist. crowds from all Judea and Jerusalem are coming to you. what do you tell them about yourself?
options: that you are the one they've been waiting for.

original.note: Greek: the beginning of the good news — the first words of Mark.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gospel is one of the four books about Jesus.
what it means: good news, and Mark's opening claim that the real good news starts here.

what a scholar hears: euangelion was imperial language; the Priene inscription (9 BC) calls Augustus's birthday the beginning of good tidings. some early manuscripts lack 'the Son of God' in Mark 1:1.

notes: Camp 4 opening: review marks the shift.
Markan priority ('most scholars think') and Mark as the shortest gospel: confirm.
Priene calendar inscription (9 BC): calls the birthday of Augustus the beginning of good tidings (euangelia) for the world. Confirm paraphrase.
Elijah allusion: 2 Kings 1:8 (hairy man, leather girdle) and Malachi 4:5 (Elijah before the day of the LORD). Confirm.
Textual note: 'the Son of God' absent from the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and some other witnesses. Confirm.
Mark 1:2–3 conflates Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3; the KJV reads 'in the prophets' (other manuscripts 'in Isaiah the prophet'). Not raised in the script; a Keeper may want it later.
